title: The thing founders should learn isn't fundraising, it's learning to say no
dek: Beyond Yoga founder Michelle Wahler says you don't have to raise money or plan an exit — just build a business that's sustainable. Her husband stopped her from making swimwear and forced her to perfect one pair of leggings first.
why: All three callers' problems are concrete: conversion for adult study-abroad trips, a craftsman winning back old clients, a small brand selling emotion online. The answers are concrete too, not chicken soup.
who: Early founders agonizing over whether to raise, small business owners who live on craft and word of mouth, and anyone selling high-ticket experiential products who's stuck on conversion.
skip: The opening, where Michelle talks about her life after leaving Beyond Yoga, is low on information and can be skipped.

points.h: You don't have to raise, and you don't have to plan an exit
points.body: Michelle says the advice entrepreneurs hear most often is ‘you have to raise’, and she thinks that's BS. Her logic: once you bring in investors, the exit becomes the company's focus and the company's trajectory changes with it. She suggests first figuring out what drives you and what you want the business to become, then building a sustainable business instead of staring at an exit. She adds: you don't have to be the next Anthropic, and you probably won't be, but there's nothing wrong with a smaller business that supports you and gives you freedom in your life.

points.h: Screen people first, then let them book a call
points.body: Carrie's adult study-abroad courses average $6,200. Plenty of people express interest, open the emails, book calls — but they don't enroll, and neither deadlines nor discounts help. Michelle's suggestion is to add a few screening questions before ‘book a call’: Are you ready for a seven-day immersive experience? Are you willing to spend money on this once-in-a-lifetime investment in yourself? Are you a lifelong learner? If every answer is an enthusiastic yes, then we'll talk. That filters out the calls that were never going to convert.

points.h: Not putting up the Eiffel Tower is what lost her people
points.body: Carrie explains why the site doesn't show the Eiffel Tower: the travel market is crowded, and she wants to emphasize that this is an educational experience, a community of lifelong learners, not sightseeing. Michelle pushes back: the first two images on the site are a group of people looking at a map and a group of people in a classroom, and those images could be anywhere. You should show people, at a glance, the thing that exists only here. Guy adds another layer: what actually stops people from hitting the enroll button is the anxiety of ‘I won't know a single person’, so sell the cohort — eight days with ten equally curious people — and put up testimonials like ‘I was nervous at first too, I almost didn't go’.

points.h: Go to retirement communities and sign up four or five at once
points.body: Michelle offers a channel idea: partner with high-end bespoke travel agencies, or with high-end independent living communities. She uses her own 79-year-old mother as an example — her mother lives in an independent living community, surrounded by retired people who are all looking for something exciting to do, but who are afraid to go alone. Partner with communities like that and you might get four or five people signing up together at once, which is great top of funnel. Guy also suggests counterintuitively trying print media, like the New York Review of Books or the London Review of Books — spend a thousand dollars on a small ad, and the readership is exactly people over fifty with obvious intellectual curiosity.

points.h: Fix the process first, then win back old clients one at a time
points.body: Grace makes custom upholstered furniture. When she started in 2021 she was flooded with demand, promised timelines too fast, and left some interior designers embarrassed in front of their clients. Michelle says the relationships can be rebuilt, but only if you get operations in order first — if you fail to deliver a second time, the relationship is finished for good. The method: make a list, go one by one, start with the smallest client, learn from that before moving up, and don't contact the second until you've won back the first. Guy calls it a ‘second first impression’: don't open by asking someone to trust you again, let them see what you're making now, and ask for a small project first.

points.h: Build buffer into your quotes and deliver early
points.body: Michelle's concrete approach for Grace: first time your own process like an assembly line to learn your real capacity, then deliberately add buffer to the delivery expectations you give designers — enough buffer, but not so much that it scares them off. That way you work toward a target of two weeks early. If you really do finish two weeks early, call the designer and say ‘we can deliver early, or we can hold it for you’ — that's a huge plus. And if the budget was off and you genuinely need a few extra days, that two-week buffer absorbs it. Either way you win.

points.h: What the website is missing isn't design, it's story
points.body: Angel makes handmade soap with a stone hidden inside that corresponds to an emotion, paired with an affirmation. At markets everyone says it's wonderful; online it doesn't sell. Michelle says she opened the website and couldn't find a story — even the about page was empty when you clicked in — and that's the first thing to fix today. She also points out that every product is called a ‘self-care kit’, when it should just say rose quartz, tiger eye, with a note next to it saying whether that stone corresponds to love or energy, instead of making people click into each one. It's also a perfect gifting scenario, so the copy can extend from ‘a moment for yourself’ to ‘for someone who deserves a moment more’.

points.h: You're selling a ritual, not soap
points.body: Guy uses the Calgon ad from his childhood as an analogy: a woman washing her hair in the bathtub, then the shot cuts to the Caribbean. He says what Angel is really selling is that ritual — wherever you are, these five minutes of product can take you away — and that costs nothing, it just requires changing how you express it on the website, then using that to tell the story across every channel. Michelle adds the conversion formula: explain the ingredients and build trust, tell the story, show the product — all three have to be true at once for the sale to happen, because this is something you put on your skin.

Guy's phrase for re-approaching an old client not with an apology but by showing new work to rebuild the impression.
The principle Michelle keeps repeating: leave room when you promise, exceed expectations when you deliver.

quotes.text: I don't think you need to raise money. And I feel like everybody tells you that you have to.

You don't have to be the next anthropic and you probably won't be, but there's nothing wrong with building a smaller sustainable business that gives you the freedom to live your life and support yourself.
I think a very important motto is under promise and over deliver.
But don't reach out to the second one until you've won the first one back.
I don't think it's a matter of, like, asking somebody to trust you. It's not like saying, hey, please trust me again. I think it's more about showing them what you do.
You're trying to tell a story on your website. You're trying to gain trust and you're trying to showcase product. And when all three of those things are working, that's when you convert a sale.
what you say no to is almost more important than what you say yes to. So don't forget to say no.
